title: Casper and the Deadline
premise: Kestrel Ishikawa, a financial-crimes investigator who has spent years laundering their own identity as carefully as any criminal launders money, is living under a protected alias when the safe house appears on a real-estate site — interior photos included. The listing is a message from Vesper Halloway, the estate architect behind a trillion-dollar inheritance scheme that three governments are about to legitimize at an upcoming summit. As Kestrel races to expose the scheme's ledger — hidden inside the estate of Kestrel's supposedly dead mother — they are hunted by an assassin who turns out to be the sibling Kestrel was erased to protect. In the end, Kestrel chooses exposure over safety, testifying at the summit and surrendering their false name, discovering that identity was never something to hide but something to claim.
about_author: Paloma Amberdale is the pen name of a former compliance analyst who spent a decade tracing money through shell companies before turning to fiction. They write thrillers about people whose paper lives and real lives refuse to match.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Scrolling property listings out of habit, Kestrel finds their own safe house for sale — with photos showing their go-bag on the bed. Panic masked as procedure: they sweep for bugs, burn nothing, decide to run. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out of a life built on invisibility.

chapters.title: Clean Money, Dirty Hands
chapters.summary: Flashback-woven chapter in Kestrel's POV establishing their day job investigating Halloway Structured Estates, and the polished lie of their alias 'Maren Cole.' A colleague mentions the summit's asset-amnesty framework. Beat: competence as armor, dread underneath.

chapters.title: The Broker Who Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Kestrel traces the listing to a boutique agency and confronts the broker, who has no memory of taking it on but perfect records of doing so. POV shifts briefly to the assassin, watching from a parked car, noting Kestrel's tradecraft with professional respect. Beat: being seen for the first time in years.

chapters.title: Go-Bag Doctrine
chapters.summary: Kestrel runs — new city, cash, burner phone — but every safe contact already knows the alias Maren. Someone upstream sold the legend. Interleaved: the assassin reports to Vesper Halloway, who says only 'let them run.' Beat: paranoia sharpening into clarity.

chapters.title: Mother's Estate
chapters.summary: Following the money backward, Kestrel finds the listing photos were shot inside properties all tied to the Ishikawa family estate declared abandoned after their mother's death. A probate clerk lets slip the estate was never settled — someone has been paying its taxes for twenty years. Beat: grief reopening like a wound.

chapters.title: Vesper
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV. Charismatic, patient, she reviews the amnesty summit agenda and her plan to launder a dynasty's fortune into legitimacy. She orders the assassin not to kill Kestrel yet — 'they're the only one who can open the vault.' Beat: villainy as architecture, not rage.

chapters.title: Three Governments, One Form
chapters.summary: Kestrel tries going official, approaching a summit liaison under a third identity. The liaison is interested — until Kestrel's file comes back pre-flagged as unstable. The system isn't broken; it was written by Halloway's firm. Beat: institutional betrayal.

chapters.title: The Assassin's Ledger
chapters.summary: Assassin POV. Their target dossier on Kestrel contains a childhood photo and a name they shouldn't know. They begin pulling their own thread instead of following orders, finding their own adoption records purchased through a Halloway trust. Beat: the hunter realizing they are also prey.

chapters.title: Dead Drop, Live Wire
chapters.summary: Kestrel arranges a meet with the assassin using the estate's old family signals — a chalk mark only an Ishikawa would know. The assassin comes anyway. Knife-edge conversation; neither gives their name; both leave alive on purpose. Beat: recognition without confession.

chapters.title: What the Photos Showed
chapters.summary: Kestrel re-examines the listing photos and realizes the interiors include rooms that no longer exist — the house was photographed decades ago. The listing wasn't surveillance; it was an invitation home. Beat: horror softening into terrible homesickness.

chapters.title: Amnesty
chapters.summary: Summit prep intensifies; governments prepare to bless Halloway's framework as anti-corruption reform. Kestrel's former colleague is reassigned after asking questions. Kestrel realizes the deadline isn't the summit — it's ratification night, when the ledger becomes legally untouchable. Beat: clock now audible.

chapters.title: The Vault Under the Orchard
chapters.summary: Kestrel breaks into the decaying family estate and finds the physical ledger vault beneath the orchard — sealed with biometric locks keyed to bloodline. It needs two Ishikawas. Beat: hope arriving shaped like a problem.

chapters.title: Sibling Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Assassin POV. Confronting their handler, they learn the truth: they and Kestrel were split as children, one erased, one weaponized, both assets of the same trust. They choose to defect — or so they tell themselves. Beat: identity cracking open.

chapters.title: Two Keys
chapters.summary: Kestrel and the assassin meet deliberately this time, names exchanged in the orchard rain. Distrust, then grudging partnership. They plan the vault opening for the night before ratification. Beat: family found in the least likely person.

chapters.title: Halloway's Offer
chapters.summary: Halloway intercepts Kestrel personally — no guards, just tea and terms: walk away wealthy, with a new name of their choosing, or be discredited as the investigator who fabricated everything. Kestrel refuses. Beat: temptation made genuinely attractive, then refused.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Retaliation: Kestrel's remaining aliases are burned simultaneously across three jurisdictions; arrest warrants bloom. The siblings go fully underground, moving through smuggling routes the assassin once used for work. Beat: fugitive intimacy, fear braided with resolve.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Price
chapters.summary: Inside the vault, the ledger proves everything — and implicates their mother, who built the first shell for Halloway before trying to stop her. The inheritance theme lands: what they've inherited is complicity as much as evidence. Beat: disillusionment, then decision to publish it all anyway.

chapters.title: Ratification Eve
chapters.summary: Summit security locks down the city; the siblings smuggle copies to journalists while Halloway's people sweep for them. The assassin draws on old contacts to buy one hour of blackout in the summit's network. Beat: coiled, breath-held preparation.

chapters.title: The Summit Floor
chapters.summary: Climax begins. Kestrel walks into the summit under a journalist's borrowed credential as the vote opens. Halloway spots them mid-chamber. The assassin triggers the blackout, and Kestrel takes the floor during thirty seconds of darkness. Beat: terror transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Thirty Seconds of Dark
chapters.summary: Climax. In the dark, Kestrel broadcasts the ledger to every delegate's terminal and names their own true name aloud — first time in twenty years. Lights return to chaos: delegates reading, Halloway composed but cornered, security converging. Beat: exposure as liberation.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Annotated
chapters.summary: Falling action. Halloway arrested as three governments scramble; the amnesty collapses. Kestrel, in custody then cleared, declines witness protection — no more hidden names. The assassin, legally nonexistent, chooses to remain so, but stays close. Beat: exhaustion edged with peace.

chapters.title: Deed to the House
chapters.summary: Resolution. Kestrel buys the safe house — the real one, openly, under their own name — and unpacks the go-bag for good. Final image: a new listing photo, taken by Kestrel, of light in the kitchen. Beat: identity claimed, home chosen, story closed.
